name: Exosome treatments

card.summary: Stem-cell-derived vesicle serums applied after microneedling; exosome biology is well studied, but cosmetic use is unproven and the FDA treats exosome products as drugs.
card.aka: Exosome serum; stem cell exosomes; extracellular vesicle skincare
card.note: The FDA has stated exosome products are drugs requiring pre-market approval and has reported patient injuries linked to injections.

quick.overview:
Exosomes are tiny membrane-bound vesicles released by cells, and cosmetic products marketed as exosome serums use vesicles from sources such as stem cells, often applied after microneedling to skin said to be aging or scarred.

Laboratory research on exosomes is extensive, but clinical trials of cosmetic exosome products are few and small, and registered trials in skin aging and hair loss are early-stage or have ended without results being listed.
quick.mechanism: Exosomes carry proteins, lipids and nucleic acids between cells, and researchers study them as signalling carriers. Proponents of cosmetic use propose that these cargoes can signal skin cells to repair; whether functional transfer of this kind occurs in humans is described by Wikipedia as having limited definitive evidence.
quick.risks: In late 2019 the FDA issued an advisory about noncompliant exosome marketing and about patient injuries linked to exosome injections, stating that exosomes are drug products requiring pre-market approval. Wikipedia describes ongoing unapproved marketing of cosmetic exosome products. Products differ in source and purity.

lead: Exosome treatments are cosmetic or medical-aesthetic products that use exosomes, small extracellular vesicles of roughly 30 to 150 nanometres released by cells, typically derived from stem cells and applied to the skin, frequently after microneedling [1]. They are marketed for skin rejuvenation, scarring and hair.

Exosome biology is a major research field. A 2007 paper showed that exosomes from mast cells carry mRNAs and microRNAs that can be transferred between cells [2], and reviews describe exosomes as mediators of cell-to-cell communication [3][4]. A position statement from the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles notes that the field uses many overlapping terms for vesicle types and sets minimal reporting standards [5].

Cosmetic use is far less studied. Registered trials of exosomes with microneedling for skin aging and for hair loss exist, but no published results were identified for this article [6][7][8]. The FDA has said exosome products are drugs requiring pre-market approval [1].

The idea behind the appearance use is a chain: vesicles carrying growth-related signals are placed on skin that microneedling has just opened with tiny channels, in the hope that the skin responds by repairing itself, which proponents associate with smoother texture, less visible scarring and denser-looking hair [1][11][12]. Providers and brands describe this as a 'cell-free' alternative to stem cell treatment.

paras: Exosomes are formed inside the endosomal system of cells and released when a multivesicular body fuses with the cell membrane. Their cargo includes proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, and varies with the cell of origin [1]. Wikipedia notes it is unclear whether exosomes have unique functions or can be reliably separated from other vesicles, and that the broader term extracellular vesicle is often more accurate [1][5].
Exosomes were first identified in maturing reticulocytes in 1983 by two research groups, and the term was applied to this vesicle type in 1987 [1].

sections.h: Use in skin and hair care
paras: In aesthetic practice, exosome serums are most often paired with microneedling, a procedure in which a device with fine needles punctures the skin repeatedly to stimulate repair; microneedling is used for scars and acne marks and, in some studies cited on Wikipedia, has been combined with minoxidil for hair loss [11]. The serum is applied while the micro-channels are open, on the reasoning that this lets vesicles reach the dermis. Practitioners and brands market the combination for photoaging, scarring, skin texture and hair thinning.

Hair loss is the other main area. Androgenetic alopecia is driven by dihydrotestosterone-mediated follicle miniaturisation, and reviews of treatment options list approved drugs and light-based therapies as the established options, with newer biologic approaches under study [12][13]. Laboratory work has reported that exosomes from mesenchymal stem cells primed with rapamycin enhanced hair regrowth in animal models, a preclinical finding [14]. Similarly, a 2019 laboratory and animal study found that exosomes from fibroblast spheroids improved skin photoaging after needle-free delivery [15].

No published clinical trial results of cosmetic exosome products were loaded for this article. Registered studies include a completed phase 4 trial of topical exosomes applied with a microneedling device for facial skin aging in 30 participants, with no results listed in the registry entry [6]; an early-phase trial of exosomes for hair loss in 16 participants that was terminated [7]; and a 20-participant study of exosomes for prevention of hair loss with unknown status [8].

Outside cosmetics, Wikipedia cites animal findings, such as faster wound healing in rats with exosomes from oral keratinocytes, and early clinical trials of other exosome-based therapies, and says many therapeutic applications are preclinical or early-stage [1]. Wikipedia also states that definitive evidence of functional RNA transfer by exosomes in mammals remains limited [1].

Preclinical work is more extensive. Reviews describe exosome-based interventions in diabetic wound healing as a cell-free regenerative approach under investigation, and animal studies report effects on hair regrowth and photoaged skin [14][15].

Cosmetic exosome products differ in cell source (stem cells from fat, bone marrow or umbilical tissue, or cultured fibroblasts), in how vesicles are isolated and in what they contain. The International Society for Extracellular Vesicles guidelines set minimal reporting standards because isolation methods and nomenclature vary widely between laboratories [5]. A review of challenges in exosome therapy lists standardisation of collection, regulatory classification and delivery as open issues [16]. Products sold for skincare are not necessarily characterised to those standards.

According to Wikipedia, in late 2019 the FDA issued an advisory about noncompliant exosome marketing and patient injuries in Nebraska linked to exosome injections, and stated that exosomes are drug products requiring pre-market approval. In 2020 the agency cautioned firms about marketing exosomes for COVID-19 and other conditions. Wikipedia describes continued unapproved marketing in US clinics, including cosmetic skincare claims, though that later statement is not well cited [1].

The FDA's public safety notification of December 6, 2019 stated that there are no FDA-approved exosome products, that some clinics were offering unreviewed exosome products with unsubstantiated claims, and that serious adverse events had been reported in Nebraska patients treated with such products. The agency said exosome products used to treat disease are generally regulated as drugs and biologics requiring premarket review, and encouraged patients to ask whether the FDA has reviewed a treatment and to report adverse events through MedWatch [10]. Because microneedling is a skin-puncturing procedure, public-health reports on blood-borne infections after non-medical vampire facials, in which microneedling is combined with a blood product, illustrate the infection-control considerations of any such procedure done outside a clinical setting [11].

Exosome serums are categorised on the wiki under hardmaxx as an add-on to microneedling and similar procedures, and sit alongside PRP, polynucleotides and other 'regenerative' skin treatments in aesthetic clinics. A forum thread on a bodybuilding site quotes a clinic's description of a related protocol in which a person's own stem cells are cultured, the secreted vesicles collected and then re-injected intravenously, as part of whole-body longevity treatments; this is a different use from the topical skin serums described above.[9]

chain: Microneedling creates micro-channels in the skin
Exosome serum is applied to the treated area
Vesicle cargo is proposed to signal skin or follicle cells toward repair
Smoother, more even skin or denser-looking hair is the intended result
angle.text: Exosome serums are applied to skin right after a microneedling session, or injected by clinics, with the aim of improving texture, scars, fine lines or hair density. The visible benefit is the goal rather than a documented outcome of published cosmetic trials.
